aka: Priory Church of St. Anthony, Lenton

stories.text: Henry II gave Lenton Priory an eight-day fair for St Martin's Day, which Henry III lengthened to twelve, with tolls paid to the monks for every booth. The fair outlived the priory: in 1584, when servants of Mary, Queen of Scots came, it was a horse fair, and by the 17th century it was known as a great fair for all sorts of horses. In the 19th century farmers and horse dealers still came.

William Peverel founded a priory of Cluniac monks at Lenton in about 1102–08, and richly endowed it. In February 1538 its last prior, Nicholas Heath, and many of his monks were thrown into prison, accused of high treason. The prior, eight monks and four Lenton labourers were executed, in Nottingham and in front of the priory, and the priory was dissolved that year. Little is left: the Priory Church of St Anthony is thought to keep part of its hospital chapel.

stories.text: The first Albert Hall, a temperance hall by Watson Fothergill, opened in 1876 and from 1902 was a Wesleyan Methodist mission; it burnt down on 22 April 1906. Albert Edward Lambert designed the present hall, dedicated in 1909, and it stayed a Methodist mission until 1982. It is now a conference and concert venue.

Helen Watts, the daughter of the vicar of Lenton, joined Nottingham's suffragettes after hearing Christabel Pankhurst speak in 1907. In 1909 she served a month in Holloway, was arrested here at the Albert Hall in July and let go without charge, and went on hunger strike in Leicester gaol.

stories.text: On the night of 8–9 May 1941 the Luftwaffe bombed Nottingham. Firefighters saved St Mary's Church after an incendiary burned through its roof; three Boots factories, in Poplar Street, Island Street and Station Street, were on fire; University College and the Shakespeare Street chapel were hit. The worst loss was at the Co-op bakery on Meadow Lane, where 49 people died. In all, 159 people were killed that night.
